references.text: The Lord judges the evil servant by his own words. The parallel is found in Matt 25:26-27, where the master in the parable of the talents similarly confronts the lazy servant with his own logic: 'You knew that I reap where I have not sown?'
The principle that a person's own words are used as judgment against him. Job 15:6: 'Your own mouth condemns you, not I; your own lips testify against you.'
David uses the Amalekite's own words to judge him. 2 Sam 1:16: 'Your blood be on your own head! For your own mouth has testified against you.' The same principle of being judged by one's own words.
Jesus teaches that people will be judged by their own words. Matt 12:37: 'For by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.'

Rom 3:19 states that the law speaks so that 'every mouth may be stopped, and all the world may become guilty before God.' God's judgment brings humanity to silence – they have no excuse, just as the evil servant is judged by his own confession.

Luke 12:47-48 emphasizes that whoever knows their master's will but does not act accordingly will be punished severely. The evil servant in Luke 19 admitted he knew the master's character yet acted anyway – which intensifies the judgment.

Matt 25:24-25 is the close parallel where the servant says exactly the same thing: that the master is a harsh man who reaps where he has not sown. The servant uses this as an excuse for his laziness, but the master turns the words against him.
